prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, trapping atoms at a magic wavelength to reach fractional frequency uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I moved my own opening ranking so that the optical lattice clock is now my preferred single-achievement prize. The physics is original (the magic-wavelength condition cancels the light shift of the trapping field), it is quantitatively rigorous, and every systematic (blackbody shift, collisions, lattice light shifts) has been controlled and cross-checked in independent laboratories in Tokyo, Boulder, Paris, Germany and elsewhere, with clock comparisons agreeing near the 1e-18 level. That is the kind of robust, reproducible, measurement-grounded result I value. It also reaches fundamental physics: tests of constant variation, searches for dark matter, relativistic redshift over millimetres, and the pending redefinition of the second. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori proposed and first demonstrated the scheme, and Ye drove it to record accuracy and the many-body regime. It also had the broadest opening support, ranked by seven of eight members and in the top three by four, including two first places. It follows 2025 (circuit tunnelling) without repeating it and is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that it is a precision-measurement achievement built on ground already recognised by the frequency-comb (2005) and ion-control (2012) prizes, so it may be read as incremental. The redefinition of the second has not happened, and the credited names omit early contributors such as Lemonde and Takamoto. Against my own earlier first choice, topological insulators (B058), the physics of a new class of quantum matter is arguably deeper, so if the committee values a new state of matter over an instrument I would not object to that outcome.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first because Katori's proposal and Ye's accuracy records are thoroughly confirmed by several independent labs, and sees no conflict with the 2005 comb prize.
responses.response: I agree on both points and my revised view rests on his argument: independent reproduction at SYRTE, PTB, RIKEN and JILA is what makes this robust. I would qualify the claim of no overlap, since Ye worked in the Hall comb environment and the committee will have to word the citation so that it clearly honours the lattice-clock concept rather than comb metrology.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the magic-wavelength idea is a genuinely new atomic-structure insight and that two names give a fair, clean configuration.
responses.response: I agree that two names suffice. As a theorist in electronic structure I would add that the magic-wavelength condition depends on accurate polarizabilities, so calculation and measurement have supported each other. I defer to her on atomic structure; my one concern is that this strength is also why some will call it refined atomic physics rather than a new phenomenon.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the architecture behind superconducting processors, and Cirac-Zoller second as foundational theory that became experimental platforms.
responses.response: I take circuit QED seriously, but I disagree on timing and attribution. It follows the 2025 circuit prize very closely, and the supplied names omit Wallraff, whose strong-coupling experiment is central, so I place it behind the clock. For Cirac-Zoller I share Lindroth's concern that a theory-only prize overlaps with Wineland's 2012 prize, and I would want the experimental realisations weighed first.

responses.point: Danielsson puts precision CMB mapping first and IceCube second, as clear, instrument-driven discoveries about the universe that are overdue.
responses.response: I defer to him and Pearce on astrophysics and astroparticle physics. I note that the CMB trio is contested between WMAP and Planck and leaves out instrument builders, whereas IceCube's attribution seems tractable but needs expert checking against AMANDA and Baikal. I do not regard either as stronger than the clock on robustness, but I would not oppose IceCube if the committee's experts confirm the credit.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks KPZ first as a clean universality class with exact solutions and experimental confirmation, and ranks topological insulators fourth.
responses.response: KPZ is elegant and the Tracy-Widom confirmation in liquid-crystal turbulence is convincing, but the original 1986 paper includes Parisi, who is absent from the supplied names and already a 2021 laureate, so a fair prize for the discovery is difficult to construct. I agree with his assessment of the topological insulator candidacy and keep it as my first alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether early contributors (Lemonde, Takamoto, others) deserve a place that the two-name configuration excludes.
Whether topological insulators (B058) can be given a fair three-person split given the omission of Zhang, Bernevig and Hughes.
Whether the committee prefers a new state of matter over a precision instrument this year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: I am at Uppsala and my connections (Johansson, Los Alamos, Bergman, Bergqvist, Hellsvik, Delin) are not linked to any shortlisted candidate. I served as Chair for the 2025 prize.
